But the inhabitants, with their families and all their movable property, hid in the forests. The punitive expedition destroyed the auls, and the crops it ravaged and trampled down"[33]. On 16 July Colonel Nakashidze entered Cheberloy in two columns: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write - he "destroyed 5 villages, including the auls of Makazhoy and Sadoy, arrested up to a thousand people and seized a large number of livestock"[19]. On 14 August the troops took the aul of Dyshni-Vedeno at the walls of the Vedeno fortress - the insurgents, according to historian A. I. Ismailova, defended every saklia (a highlander's house) "despite the murderous artillery fire"[33]. October 1905 C1175 Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army At the end of 1906 a punitive detachment of the Russian Empire, with artillery and Cossacks, was restoring imperial power in the Vedeno okrug: "the villages of Nizhaloy, Nokhch-Keloy, Khoy and Makazhoy, whose residents stubbornly refused to submit, were subjected to artillery bombardment"; it was noted that as a result of the punitive expedition "...the greater part of the population of the Vedeno okrug, seized by panic, fled to the mountains, where it suffers hunger and cold"; several hundred people were arrested, most of them convicted and exiled[19]. In August 1908 the village of Tsatsan-Yurt was subjected to an "execution" with mass searches[19]. January 1919 C0074 Second Armed Invasion and Resource Depletion (1919) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0010 Regular Army Use of military units and food requisition detachments for forcible raids on Ukrainian villages to confiscate grain[34]. February 1919 C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army At the end of February 1919 four regiments of the Volunteer Army - the division of General Shatilov - attacked the village of Goity with artillery, for its refusal to hand over the Red Army men sheltering there; detachments from the surrounding villages came to its aid, and the Denikinites retreated toward Grozny[19]. On 23 March the army struck from Grozny at Gudermes[19]. From 27 to 30 March battles raged for Alkhan-Yurt: "The shelling of the village was conducted by 24 guns and an armored train that had taken position near the Ermolovskaya stanitsa... the village was captured"; more than 400 of its defenders died[19]. For failure to fulfill the demand to return captured Cossacks the army stormed Tsatsan-Yurt - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "On 9 April 1919 the White troops attacked and by nightfall captured the village of Tsatsan-Yurt. In the course of the fierce battle more than 500 people died on the Chechen side, including over 400 Tsatsan-Yurt villagers proper"[19]. In October the command threw against Chechnya a force of 15 thousand soldiers and officers taken off the advance on Moscow: "On 5 October stubborn three-day battles began for Chechen-Aul, after which the villages situated near the railway were subjected to a new devastation"[19]. July 1925 C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Through the resisting villages the troops moved in raids with house-to-house searches and arrests. The instruction on mass searches, issued for the operation by the staff of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB), ordered houses to be cordoned off and everyone found in them to be detained and searched, and speaks of arrests in points 7 and 8: "All who counteract in one measure or another the successful conduct of the mass operation are brought to account and arrested", "Malicious concealers of weapons are arrested"; of what was taken during a search the same document says: "During searches and arrests only all correspondence is taken, including correspondence in the Arabic language, as well as all weapons found during the search"[35]. The information department of the OGPU, in its "Survey of the Political Condition of the USSR for September 1925" stamped "Top Secret", summed up the operation with the words "On our side losses are 20 men"[36], and reported nothing about the killed and wounded in the shelled and bombed auls. The count of losses for the operation as a whole is given by historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov from a journal publication of 1995: six killed civilians, 30 wounded, a further 12 killed assigned to the "bandits", with the troops' own losses at five killed and nine wounded[19]. January 1944 C0084 Suppression of UPA Resistance and Operation "Vistula" (1944–1951) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services Regular chekist-military operations by the NKVD and MGB to sweep western Ukrainian villages: the People's Commissar of Internal Affairs of the Ukrainian SSR T. Strokach personally "directed and coordinated operational-chekist operations to liquidate the underground of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists and units of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, and mass deportations of the population in Western Ukraine"[37]. Already "on April 5, 1944, on the basis of a directive of the People's Commissariat of Internal Affairs of the USSR, a scheme of arrests and deportation of OUN–UPA members was worked out"[38]. May 1953 C0086 Suppression of the GULAG Uprisings (1953–1954) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Use of regular troops and tanks to suppress revolts of Ukrainian political prisoners in the concentration camp system. In Kengir, tanks crushed the unarmed: "About 200 Ukrainian women joined hands and marched against the tanks. But the tanks did not stop and one by one overcame the living phalanx. And the MVD men rushed to the barracks, shooting everyone they encountered"[39]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Кушева. title: Implantation of Officials and Military Personnel, technique T0041
content: Implantation of Officials and Military Personnel Aggressors may carry out the mass relocation of their administrative and military apparatus to colonized territories. Stationing regular military garrisons and appointing loyal officials from the metropole allows the colonizer to establish strict physical and bureaucratic oversight, preemptively suppress nascent resistance on the ground, and integrate the region into its own state system, displacing local institutions of self-governance. ID: T0041 ⓘ Tactic: Persistence ⓘ Peoples: Nokhchi (Chechens), Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1588 C1110 Founding and Fortification of the Terek Town (1588–1623) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army A permanent military contingent maintained at state expense was stationed in the territory: historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova quotes a tsar's decree according to which «in 1623, «upon the petition of the Terek and Greben Cossacks», a tsar's decree was sent to the Terek ordering the payment of salaries to 30 atamans and 470 rank-and-file Cossacks»[1]. New personnel were also sent in to hold the positions: historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova notes that «in 1589, soon after the town was built, 800 streltsy and Cossacks were to be sent there from Astrakhan, but the Astrakhan voivode sent only 600 men»[1]. October 1659 C0004 Pereiaslav Articles (1659) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army After forcing the signing of the treaty, Moscow moved to the direct occupation of the autonomy's living space. The articles codified the expansion of the military presence: "besides Kyiv, tsarist voivodes were introduced into Pereiaslav, Chernihiv, Nizhyn, Bratslav, and Uman"[2] – garrisons headed by voivodes ensured physical control over the territory from within. September 1665 C0024 The Moscow Articles of Ivan Briukhovetsky (1665) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army Expansion of the military occupation of the autonomy: in addition to reinforcing the garrisons of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Pereiaslav, and Nizhyn, "Russian military garrisons headed by voivodes were introduced into Poltava, Kremenchuk, Novhorod-Siverskyi, Oster, Kaniv, and other cities, as well as into Kodak in the Liberties of the Zaporozhian Host"[3] – the upkeep of the troops was placed on Ukrainian taxpayers. January 1687 C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army To ensure constant armed oversight of the autonomy's top leadership and to prevent uprisings, the Tsardom of Muscovy stationed its regular troops directly in the hetman's capital: "with the hetman in Baturyn, for his protection and safety, there shall be a Muscovite streltsy regiment..."[4]. January 1700 C0011 Integration Reforms of Peter I and the Great Northern War (1700–1708) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army The strangulation of the autonomy's economy through the system of billeting the regular army: "And when the kompaniytsi and serdiuks stand in winter quarters... 24 commoners feed a single kompaniyets without any excuses"[4][5]. July 1709 C0016 The Reshetylivka Articles (1709) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Preservation of tsarist representatives' oversight of the hetmanate's administrative apparatus: the articles "fully preserved the previously established control of the tsarist regime over local financing and the functioning of the administrative apparatus"[6]. The institution of the tsar's resident was established alongside the hetman: "The first tsar's resident was stolnik A. Izmailov, who in his work was guided by official and secret tsarist articles"; the residents "were given the right to control the election and official appointments of representatives of the starshyna"[6]. January 1711 C0027 Pylyp Orlyk's Campaign in Right-Bank Ukraine (1711) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army The empire's forcible retention of the Right Bank: the Bila Tserkva fortress with its Muscovite garrison held out, and the campaign collapsed after the Tatars' betrayal – "Orlyk retreated without taking Bila Tserkva"[7], and his army disintegrated. September 1722 C1130 Construction of the Holy Cross Fortress and Forced Resettlement (1722–1724) G0009 Russian Empire S0025 Militarized Settlers Militarized Settlers of the Russian Empire were used for the mass settlement of new frontiers: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov points out that at the new fortress "1 thousand families of Cossacks from the Don are being settled"[8]. January 1736 C1134 Construction of Fortified Stanitsas, Settlement of Cossacks on the Borders, and Holding of Hostages (1736–1740) G0009 Russian Empire S0025 Militarized Settlers The Government of the Russian Empire physically enlarged the buffer zone around the territories of the Nokhchi through the mass relocation of militarized settlers: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that «1736 - from the Greben stanitsas down the Terek to Kizlyar, three new Cossack stanitsas are established: Borozdinskaya, Kargalinskaya, Dubovskaya, and from Kizlyar to the sea another 430 Cossack families are settled»[8]. June 1840 C1165 "Constriction of Chechnya from all sides": blockade, secret war, punitive expeditions and the Sunzha Line (1840-1846) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In Chechen villages the empire quartered its troops. The "Journal of military events on the left flank of the Caucasus Line" for 23 May - 6 June 1846 records: after most inhabitants of the aul of Akbulat-Yurt on the Terek had fled, ""for the protection of the remaining inhabitants of Akbulat-Yurt and in order to use the direct communication with the Kumyk plain through this aul, maj.-gen. Kozlovsky stationed there one company of infantry with one gun and set up there a post of 25 mounted Kumyks"" (the Kumyks - a neighbouring Turkic people from whom the empire recruited mounted guards)[9]. A garrison in the aul is surveillance from within: the village's life went on under the daily watch of a company with a gun. October 1905 C1175 Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations In 1911 the Russian Empire appointed "government elders" in the zone of Zelimkhan's operations and put troops on the residents' own upkeep: "Military teams were sent to be quartered in the villages of Kharachoy, Dyshne-Vedeno, Mekhkety, Zavirkhi, Khattuni, Eshelkhotoy, Elistandzhi, Tauzen, Isti-Su, Mayrtup, Khoy, Ikharoy, Rigakhoy, Makazhoy, Avtury and the Varanda hamlets"[10]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write of this practice: "the sending of military units into Chechen villages was widely practiced, and their upkeep lay as a heavy burden on the local residents"[10]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Тхамокова И. title: Creation of Economic Dependence, technique T0046
content: Creation of Economic Dependence Aggressors may deliberately destroy or isolate the self-sufficient sectors of the colonized society's economy, replacing them with subsidies or critical supplies from the metropole. Artificially turning the region into a subsidized periphery critically dependent on the colonizer's external financing, energy resources, or export markets deprives the local population of the material base for political independence and makes organized protest economically impossible. ID: T0046 ⓘ Tactic: Persistence ⓘ People: Nokhchi (Chechens) Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1617 C1115 Economic Exploitation and Creation of Dependency of the Nokhchi (1617–1622) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The metropole's administration did not pay for forced labor and withheld food provisions for five years: a memorandum from the Posolsky Prikaz (Ambassadorial Office) to the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace records a complaint that the subordinate Okochans of Tersky Town «were not given the sovereign's grain allowance for the past years — for the 125th, and the 126th, and the 127th, and the 128th, and the 129th year»[1]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Кушева. title: Support for Separatism, technique T0012
content: Support for Separatism Aggressors may covertly or openly finance, arm, and politically support radical groups advocating the secession of part of a sovereign state's territory. Artificially inflaming internal conflicts from the outside weakens state institutions, destabilizes the region, and creates a convenient pretext for the colonizer's subsequent open intervention under the guise of a peacekeeping operation or the protection of an allegedly oppressed minority. ID: T0012 ⓘ Tactic: Preparation for Seizure ⓘ People: Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1918 C0073 Artificial Separatism and the Dismemberment of Territories (January – March 1918) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0009 Diplomacy Political and military support for local radicals (the Artem group) in proclaiming a republic not subordinate to Kyiv[1]. September 2004 C0096 Election Interference and Countering the "Orange Revolution" (2004) G0011 Russian Federation S0009 Diplomacy The instigation of the threat of splitting the country in response to the protests: at the congress in Sievierodonetsk on November 28, 2004, Regions faction leader R. Bohatyriova gave a direct promise of a separatist referendum - "we will not go to it with you, we will hold a referendum on the creation of a South-Eastern state (ovation, applause)"[2]. The presence of Russian officials lent this Moscow's sanction: the mayor of Moscow Yu. Luzhkov reminded the hall from the rostrum that "our President of Russia Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin was the first to congratulate Viktor Fedorovych Yanukovych on his victory"[2]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Лариса Якубова. title: Bribery of Elites, technique T0015
content: Bribery of Elites Aggressors may use systemic corruption and the distribution of privileges, titles, and large-scale financial resources to win over members of the target state's top leadership, intelligentsia, and military ranks. This technique permeates every stage of colonization: from preparation for seizure (recruiting agents of influence) to the seizure of governance (sabotage during defense) and institutional consolidation (buying the loyalty of a puppet government). By encouraging the personal ambitions of the elite at the expense of national interests, the colonizer destroys the local population's capacity for organized resistance. ID: T0015 ⓘ Tactics: Persistence, Seizure of Governance, Preparation for Seizure ⓘ Peoples: Nokhchi (Chechens), Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1588 C1112 Beginning of the political subjugation of the Nokhchi (1588–1591) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy To secure the political subordination of the Nokhchi elite, the administration used financial incentives: historian Murat Yasar points out that «the signing of the shert went hand in hand with monetary allowances and gifts that the tsar gave to local rulers»[1]. January 1645 C1107 Bribery of Elites, Coercion into Subjecthood, and the Taking of Amanats (1645–1658) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The occupation administration handed out privileges and transferred to loyal Nokhchi leaders power over dependent people in order to win them over to its side: the register of cases of the Posolsky Prikaz for 1645 records a petition from the serving Okotsk murza Chepan Kokhostrov to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich and a report extract by the central apparatus «on granting him an increase to his salary and possession of the uzdens and «people» of his brother, murza Albir Kokhostrov»[2]. June 1672 C0025 The Konotop Articles of Ivan Samoilovych (1672) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy A wager on the estate interests of the officer class: "The Konotop Articles limited both the hetman's power and, accordingly, the autonomy of the Hetmanate, while significantly expanding the rights of the Cossack officers"[3] – by expanding the rights of the officer oligarchy at the hetman's expense, Moscow gained levers of influence over the autonomy through the hands of its own elite. January 1685 C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy To gain control over the church, Moscow applied corruption at the international level: the Kyiv metropolitanate was seized "through bribery, manipulation, and blackmail"[4]. The payment was recorded by Patriarch Dionysius of Constantinople himself in a letter to the tsars: "We have received the alms of your holy tsardom from your envoy, lord Nikita Alekseevich – three forties of sables and two hundred gold pieces"[5]. January 1687 C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy To guarantee acceptance of the treaty's enslaving terms, the tsardom bribed the local starshyna with guarantees that they would keep their offices, placing the elite's personal ambitions above national ones: "the hetman shall not remove anyone of the general starshyna from office without the will and decree of their most serene tsarist majesty..."[6]. January 1695 C0010 Azov Campaigns and Fortress Construction (1695–1700) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy The distribution of the highest imperial awards to buy the hetman's loyalty against the backdrop of Ukraine's resource exhaustion: Peter I "deigned to name me a knight of the glorious order of the holy first-called apostle of Christ, Andrew"[6][7]. January 1735 C1133 Bribery of the Nobility and Institutionalization of the Hostage System (1735) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The occupation administration of the Russian Empire bought the loyalty of the local nobility with state payments: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that, according to General-in-Chief V. Ya. Levashov, the senior Chechen prince Aidemir «was accepted into Russian subjecthood and was assigned a permanent tsarist stipend»[8], and in general «The princes and their uzdens even began to receive monetary allowances from the Russian government»[8]. January 1741 C1135 Expansion of the Bribery System and Coercion of Highland Societies into Subjecthood (1741–1748) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The occupation administration of the Russian Empire bought the loyalty of members of the local nobility with state payments: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov records «the granting of Russian stipends to 4 Chechen princes and their uzdens»[8]. January 1806 C1139 Failed Attempt to Bribe Nokhchi Elders with Economic Promises in Exchange for Allegiance (1806) G0009 Russian Empire S0009 Diplomacy The Russian Empire, through the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, addressed the elders of the Nokhchi with a proclamation offering economic benefits in exchange for accepting subjecthood and ceasing armed resistance. For submission, the elders were promised access to salt: they would be "permitted to take salt from the local salt lakes by tickets, irrevocably, paying a very small fixed price," as well as the right "to drive livestock to this side of the Terek and freely use the vacant pasture lands." The proclamation was conveyed to Chechen society and its elders (Kusu Al-Temir, Masarai, Idut), but subjecthood was not accepted; at the beginning of the following year the empire proceeded to armed invasion.[9]. The same offer is independently recorded by the imperial historian Dubrovin: the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, "promised… to release salt in unlimited quantity, for the most trifling payment; to permit the driving of livestock for pasture in wintertime to the left bank of the Terek River… and, finally, to make them equal to Russian subjects"[10]. January 1807 C1140 Bulgakov's Punitive Expedition: Devastation of Chechen Villages and Coercion into Allegiance (1807) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire bought the loyalty of Nokhchi elders in order to use them to bring recalcitrant villages into subjecthood. The commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, instructed the Andreyevo elder Hadji-Redjeb to incline the villages "into submission and subjecthood," and assigned a salary to the Chechen uzden Bik-Bulat — "I persuaded the Chechen uzden Bik-Bulat… to whom I said… a salary of 300 r. in silver per year"; for winning over the remaining villages, "about 3,000 r. in silver for bringing them into loyal subjecthood" was allocated[9]. The same bribery, from the Nokhchi side, is recorded by the historian D. A. Khozhaev: through the intermediary Hadji-Redjeb, in the name of the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, the very head of the Chechen resistance, Beibulat Taimiev, was won over and took "an oath of fidelity of subjecthood to Russia," while Hadji-Redjeb asked the generals for another 3000 rubles in silver "for bringing the remaining unpacified Chechen villages into loyal subjecthood"[11]. January 1809 C1141 Consolidation in Chechnya: Bribery of Elders, Economic Control, and Setting Neighbors against One Another (1809-1811) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire bought the loyalty of the Nokhchi elders in order to use them to incline the Chechens toward submission. To this end, the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Tormasov, through Esaul Chernov, ordered that the Chechen elders and clergy be given «250 rubles each, and others 150 silver rubles each, as a one-time payment, for which the required sum, 1,400 r. in total»[12]. Historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov notes that the colonial authorities generally acted by relying on the social elite, «bribing them with all manner of rewards and privileges for their service to the benefit of Russia»[13]. Historian D. A. Khozhaev cites the same formula with a direct indication of where the money came from: the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Tormasov, agreed «to win over the principal Chechen elders and their clergy… to give 250, and others 150 silver rubles each, and to collect the said money from their own villages» — that is, the bribery of the elite was paid for by exactions from the Chechen villages themselves[11]. January 1817 C0041 Introduction of Military Settlements and Liquidation of the Danubian Sich (1817–1828) G0009 Russian Empire S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The luring of kish otaman Hladky over to the empire's side in 1828: part of the Danubians "headed by kish otaman Y. Hladky, on May 30 (18), 1828, crossed the Kiliya mouth of the Danube, entered the port of Izmail, and joined the Russian army"[14]. September 1837 C1162 Attempted bribery of Shamil with a promise of power over Dagestan to secure his appearance before Nicholas I in Tiflis, and the summoning of the Chechen imam Tashu-Hadji (1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In September 1837, preparing Nicholas I's visit to the Caucasus, the empire tried to recruit Shamil (Shamil - imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest), offering him power and honors in exchange for subordination to the empire. General Adlerberg conveyed the emperor's will to general Rozen in a letter of 10 August 1837: to give "Shamil and his chief accomplices Tashav-Hadji, Kibit-Magomet and the Qarakh qadi Abdurrahman suggestions... to beg the mercy of appearing before the face of the Monarch Himself" in Tiflis[15]; Tashu-Hadji (sheikh, in 1834-1836 the imam of Chechnya, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance) is named first on the list. Carrying this out, general Klugenau obtained a personal meeting with Shamil on 18 September 1837 at a spring near the aul of Karanay; as recorded by Shamil's chronicler Muhammad Tahir al-Qarakhi, the general "began to speak, asking Shamil to come for a meeting with the Russian Nicholas. He asserted that the emperor would exalt him, Shamil, show him honor, and make him the administrator of the affairs of all Dagestani Muslims. From the emperor, he said, there would be no treachery"[16]. In parallel, general Feze instructed Akhmed Khan of Mekhtuli "to persuade Shamil to arrive in Tiflis by the time of His Majesty's arrival there", as general Rozen reported to Chernyshev on 25 September 1837[17], and colonel Pullo demanded of Shamil by letter that he send "to the Groznaya fortress two deputies to be presented to the Sovereign"[15]. The bribe was delivered to its addressee and rejected: on 28 September 1837 Shamil replied to Klugenau by letter - "I have resolved not to go to Tiflis even if I am cut to pieces, because I have many times seen treachery from you"[15]; neither Shamil nor Tashu-Hadji went to Tiflis. The offer to Shamil of the post of "administrator of the affairs of all Dagestani Muslims" repeated the same policy line by which the empire, in those same years, was creating loyal religious institutions (campaign C1159). June 1840 C1165 "Constriction of Chechnya from all sides": blockade, secret war, punitive expeditions and the Sunzha Line (1840-1846) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The bribery of the highland elite the empire put on a programmatic footing. War minister Chernyshev, in a secret letter to general Golovin, commander of the Separate Caucasus Corps (head of the empire's troops and administration in the Caucasus), of 19 July 1842, proposed adopting the experience of British India: "The English knew how to establish their dominion in India by political means... Should not we too try this system?"[18]. Golovin, in a reply of 28 August 1842, drew up a list of candidates for buying over from the circle of Shamil (the imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest) and requested a fund: "By inclining to our side some of the above-mentioned persons, one would greatly weaken the union of muridism... I consider it necessary for the chief authority here to have at its disposal up to 15 thousand chervonets in ready money" (chervonets - a gold coin of the empire; muridism - in the imperial lexicon, the highlanders' resistance movement)[18]. On 1 February 1844 emperor Nicholas I approved the fund above the request: by an official service letter of Chernyshev to general Neidhardt, who had replaced Golovin at the head of the empire's troops in the Caucasus, "concerning your designs for secret dealings with the highlanders" it was commanded "instead of the 10 thousand chervonets you requested for this purpose, to assign to your charge 15 thousand chervonets"[18]. For the Dargo expedition of 1845 (the imperial army's march on Shamil's residence, the aul of Dargo) historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov record a separate fund: "for the bribery of influential persons from among the highlanders, 45 thousand rubles in silver were allocated"[19]. On the Sunzha Line under construction (the chain of imperial Cossack stanitsas and fortifications on the Sunzha river) the empire bought the loyalty of individual Chechen elders. Vorontsov, viceroy and commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, wrote in a report of summer 1846 about the elder of the aul of Natkhoy-Kezhu: "I turned my particular attention to attracting Aldumov to our side. For the losses borne by him and his 4 comrades... I would consider it just to assign a reward"[18]. January 1847 C1166 "Death sentence" for Lesser Chechnya: the massacre of Duba's hamlet, forest clearings, fortresses, annihilation of the population and stanitsas on the sites of burned auls (1847-1851) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The massacre of the hamlet of naib Duba (a deputy of Imam Shamil, leader of the highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest) on 6 March 1847 was prepared by a targeted bribe inside the naib's family. Imperial officer Poltoratsky, a participant in the assault, wrote of the detachment's guide: "This was naib Duba's own nephew, bribed together with his brother for a good cut out of the pocket of Meller" - Meller-Zakomelsky, who commanded the detachment[20]. Both brothers were bought: one led the troops against his native hamlet, the other sat as a hostage in Vozdvizhenskoye - a guarantee that the guide would not change his mind. January 1852 C1167 "Neither plow nor sow": the pogrom of Chechnya, organized famine, the buying-up of elites and the institutions of subjugation (1852-1857) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The empire demonstratively rewarded defectors from the leadership of the resistance with ranks, money and land. Bata Shamurzayev, a naib of Shamil (deputy of the Imam, leader of the highlanders' resistance of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest), went over to the empire in the autumn of 1851 and received rewards. Baryatinsky, who commanded the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), in a letter to Vorontsov, viceroy in the Caucasus, of 24 February 1852, requested - "what a great reward Bata deserves, and I ask you to pardon him, then for Avtur to return him his rank and a pension of 400 rubles a year; I also ask you for an officer's rank for his son... who has often served us as a guide"[21]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "Bata Shamurzayev took an active part in the war against the Imam, was promoted to captain and awarded 500 desiatinas of land... as an example for other potential defectors"[19]. Through Bata, Vorontsov, viceroy in the Caucasus, conveyed ultimatums to the Chechens - in a letter to Baryatinsky of 21 March 1852: "I asked Bata to insistently repeat to the inhabitants of the northern part of Greater Chechnya that we will not allow them to sow or to mow, unless they declare submission"[21]. Imperial historian Volkonsky admitted the system of bribery plainly: the empire acted "through their own co-religionists and persons like Bati Shamurzov," and "not with words alone, but with something more enticing and substantial - especially in the times of Vorontsov and Baryatinsky"[22]. January 1858 C1022 Muhajirism: the expulsion of Chechens to the Ottoman Empire, the ban on return, and population replacement (1858-1872) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government General Kundukhov, until then himself head of the Chechen okrug, received from the Viceroy "a most delicate assignment – to conduct unofficial negotiations with the Turkish government on carrying out a mass resettlement of the Chechens" and a written instruction "to proceed to arouse among the Chechen population a striving to leave for Turkey"[19]. For the agitation he received 5 thousand rubles from the treasury[19]; the historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova writes of 10 thousand "for the 'discreet remuneration' of three or four persons most popular among the population, that is, for bribing influential figures"[23]; Kundukhov personally was paid 45 thousand rubles "ostensibly for property left behind in Russia," with the treasury's total expenses exceeding 130 thousand[19]. Kundukhov himself described in his memoirs the recruitment of the Chechen leadership in February 1865: having invited the naib (an administrator of a district installed by the authorities) of Lesser Chechnya Sadulla Osmanov (in other sources - Saadula Osmayev) and the elder of the Karabulak society Tsugov, he achieved that "They all agreed to resettle without the slightest objection... and swore to prepare for resettlement"[11]. Osmanov was no outside appointee: in the consolidated list of the Imamate's naibs he stands as "Saadulla Osmanov of Nikhaloy (naib of Lesser Chechnya)"[19] - a man who had fought alongside Shamil, and who for an imperial salary and land drove his own people to Turkey. The price of the purchase is visible on him too: he governed his naibstvo for eight years, received 550 desiatinas of land for his service, swore on the Quran to assist the resettlement "to the end" and undertook to lead the second wave of those departing - going ahead of the first was a condition of payment of the reward[23]. He worked in such a way that even the head of the Terek oblast, General Loris-Melikov, admitted the naib was "overdoing it," spreading distorted rumours, and wanted to rid himself as soon as possible of the too-hotheaded agitator[23]. January 1860 C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations "In 1867 alone, 8674 desiatinas (a desiatina is a little over a hectare) were transferred into private ownership across Chechnya for various kinds of 'services'" - according to historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova, 57 Chechens received it, and she names the viceroy in the Caucasus, Baryatinsky, as the initiator of the handouts[23]; the largest allotments went to the Chechen ruling families - the Taymazovs (6550 desiatinas), the Bekovich-Cherkasskys (over 6350), the Turlovs, the Eldarovs; land was also handed out to Russian officers - "Colonel Ippolitov received more than 1 thousand desiatinas of land in the Argun okrug"[19]. The hierarchy of the handouts followed estate lines: to the largest highland owners - "from 1 to 5 thousand desiatinas, depending 'on the degree of significance and the services rendered by each to the government'", to persons of the second category (the highland notability, the first being Russian nobles) - up to 1 thousand[23]. Land also paid the lower administration: "village elders received five shares each of arable and hay lands"[19], aul secretaries - up to 75 desiatinas[24]. April 1877 C1172 "Mow Down Everything, Beat and Hang Without Mercy": Suppression of the 1877 Uprising and the Executions in Grozny (1877-1878) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The starshina (headman) of Shali, Borshchik Khambulatov, who organized the repulse of the insurgents in April 1877, "was granted the rank of ensign of the militia and an annual salary of 600 rubles, and received a lifelong pension - 100 rubles a year"[19]; historian A. I. Ismailova puts the pension at "about 400 r. a year"[25]. January 2006 C0097 Gas Wars and Energy Blackmail (2006–2009) G0011 Russian Federation S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The imposition of corrupt gas-supply schemes through intermediary companies: Moscow "used a series of intermediary trading companies (Itera from 1998, Eural Trans Gas from 2003, Rosukrenergo (RUE) from 2005) to transport, and sometimes to supply, the gas to Ukraine," a practice that "was long criticized in European government circles and by corporate governance bodies (where there was concern about their opacity)"[26]. RUE's co-owner Dmytro Firtash told the US ambassador in December 2008 outright that "He acknowledged ties to Russian organized crime figure Seymon Mogilevich, stating he needed Mogilevich's approval to get into business in the first place"[27]. October 2013 C0099 Derailing the Association with the EU (2013–2014) G0011 Russian Federation S0009 Diplomacy The use of economic blackmail and promises of a loan together with a gas discount to coerce V. Yanukovych into derailing the signing of the Association Agreement with the EU: on December 17, 2013, a reduction of the gas price "to 268.5 dollars per thousand cubic meters" (instead of 410) was announced, along with the fact that "Ukraine, under the bilateral agreements, will receive 15 billion dollars from the Russian National Welfare Fund, selling Moscow its government securities for that amount." Putin stressed: "We consider this a temporary solution, bearing in mind that long-term, long-lasting agreements must and will be reached"[28]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Murat Yaşar. title: Filtration Camp System, technique T0023
content: Filtration Camp System Aggressors may create a network of official or shadow temporary detention facilities for the mass screening, interrogation, and sorting of civilians. Isolating a significant part of the local population in closed zones not regulated by law allows the colonizer to identify and physically eliminate potential participants in resistance, as well as to carry out total psychological terror against the colonized society. ID: T0023 ⓘ Tactic: Defense Impairment ⓘ People: Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: February 2022 C0103 Full-Scale Invasion (from February 24, 2022) G0011 Russian Federation S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The creation of a network of filtration camps in the occupied territories: "'filtration' is defined within the context of this report as the multi-step system Russia and its proxies have deployed in territory they currently occupy within Ukraine to register, interrogate, and, in some cases, indefinitely detain people residing there at the time Russia and its aligned forces took that locale under its control," and "there is evidence the system was created weeks before the invasion began and likely grew following Russia's capture of Mariupol in April 2022"[1]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); title: Justification Through Religion, technique T0024
content: Justification Through Religion Aggressors may use religious rhetoric and institutions to provide ideological justification for expansion. The seizure of territories is presented not as an act of armed aggression but as a sacred mission to protect co-religionists, restore canonical justice, or fulfill a divine destiny. Using such narratives allows the colonizer to morally justify the invasion in the eyes of its own society, mobilize it to support the conflict, and disguise political absorption as spiritual unification. ID: T0024 ⓘ Tactic: Legitimization of Domination ⓘ Peoples: Nokhchi (Chechens), Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1550 C1104 Religious Frontier and the Fabrication of Historical Right (1550–1721) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0008 Government The government of the Tsardom of Muscovy used religious identity and the concept of protecting co-religionists as ideological cover for military expansion: historian Michael Khodarkovsky states that the diplomatic apparatus positioned the tsar as a "universal Christian ruler who 'upheld the true Christian faith'"[1], while invasions were motivated by a "divine obligation to rescue Orthodox Christians from infidel captivity"[1]; as a result, as historian Michael Khodarkovsky summarizes, in the advance into new territories "Moscow's military and political interests could no longer be separated from the ideological and theological rhetoric of expansion"[1], because of which the North Caucasus "became a religious frontier"[2]. January 1654 C0001 Pereiaslav Council (1654) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The seizure of a neighboring state's territories was presented to the population of the Tsardom of Muscovy not as an act of political or military expansion, but as a sacred mission of protecting brothers in faith. This myth outlived the centuries: as late as 1990 Solzhenitsyn reproduced it verbatim – "The return of these lands to Russia was then perceived by everyone as REUNIFICATION"[3]. January 1674 C0006 Publication of the "Synopsis" (1674) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The imperial historical myth was directly based on religious manipulation: expansion was justified by the concept of religious unity. The author constructed an ideologeme in order "to give the Muscovite tsar the motivation to continue the struggle with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for the liberation from Catholic rule of the remaining part of the 'single Orthodox people'"[4]. January 1685 C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The annexation of the metropolitanate was disguised as the protection of co-religionists: the reform was carried out "relying on the Orthodox movement against the Turkish conquerors"[5], and "Golitsyn's main project concerning Ukraine… became the reform of the Ukrainian Orthodox church, or rather – the subordination of the Kyiv metropolitanate to the Moscow patriarch"[5][6]. January 1686 C0009 "Eternal Peace" with Poland (1686) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy The diplomatic entrenchment of spiritual expansion: Moscow secured the inclusion in the treaty of an article on the position of the Orthodox in the Commonwealth – the 1686 treaty ordered the Polish side "to inflict no oppression and no coercion toward the Roman faith or the Union"[7] – and arrogated to itself the role of protector of Orthodoxy on Polish lands, relying on the Kyiv metropolitanate already subordinated to Moscow. The treaty also secured an ecclesiastical lever: the Orthodox eparchies in the Commonwealth "according to their spiritual rank and custom, are to receive blessing and ordination from the Metropolitan of Kyiv; and this shall harm none of them in the favor of His Royal Majesty"[8] - while the Kyiv metropolitanate was already subordinated to Moscow. October 1708 C0012 Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The anathema against Mazepa was proclaimed by the tsar's direct order - "be pleased to have him, for such a deed of his, publicly cursed in the cathedral church..."[6]. Part of the Ukrainian clergy refused to accept the rite: a former Lokhvytsia archpriest said during the proclamation of the anathema, "Our Mazepa is holy and will be in heaven, and your sovereign will not"[6]. The Ecumenical Patriarchate never recognized it: "the anathema was laid on Ivan Mazepa for political reasons and had no theological or canonical justification"[9]. January 1709 C0014 Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1709) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0011 Moscow Patriarchate The use of the church as an instrument of punishment: the anathema was proclaimed by the tsar's direct order - "be pleased to have him, for such a deed of his, publicly cursed in the cathedral church..."[6]. No theological grounding was supplied for it, and part of the Ukrainian clergy refused to accept the rite: a former Lokhvytsia archpriest said during the proclamation of the anathema, "Our Mazepa is holy and will be in heaven, and your sovereign will not"[6]. January 1721 C1108 Imposition of an Image of Backwardness and the “Civilizing” Mission (1721–1800s) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The occupation administration of the Russian Empire used religious pretexts for expansion: historian Michael Khodarkovsky cites a memorandum by Governor-General P. S. Potemkin, who in 1784 declared that under the pretext of returning the highlanders to the faith and sending priests to them, the empire would be able to shed "the light of divine bliss among all the peoples scattered in the mountains"[2]. January 1877 C0064 Russo-Turkish War and Pan-Slavism (1877–1878) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government The ideological justification of a war of conquest by religion and Pan-Slavism: per Dostoevsky, "by Russia's insistence and blood the Slavs have already been liberated… the Turkish empire no longer exists and… the Balkan peninsula is free and lives a new life"[10] – the war was given the status of a sacred mission of liberating co-religionists. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Michael Khodarkovsky. title: Forced Surrender of Fugitives and Rebels, technique T0156
content: Forced Surrender of Fugitives and Rebels Aggressors may impose on subjugated communities the obligation to refuse shelter to members of the resistance and to hand over everyone who has escaped the aggressor's power - rebels, runaway soldiers and bondsmen, prisoners. The obligation is formalized in a decree or a treaty and rests on collective liability: the whole settlement answers for harboring or for failure to inform - with fines, confiscations, devastation. In this way the aggressor destroys the very function of uncontrolled space - mountains, forests, free borderlands - as a refuge beyond its power: political scientist and anthropologist James C. Scott showed that such zones of refuge (he explicitly names the Caucasus among them) are formed by people deliberately fleeing state exactions, and political theorist Neil Roberts described flight from bondage itself as a practice of freedom - the forced surrender of fugitives strikes precisely at it. With the hands of the subjugated themselves, the aggressor turns every settlement that has yielded into a barrier against those still resisting. ID: T0156 ⓘ Tactics: Defense Impairment, Persistence ⓘ People: Nokhchi (Chechens) Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 24 July 2026 Last Modified: 24 July 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: November 1838 C1164 Forcing Chechnya into submission after the fall of Akhulgo and suppression of the general uprising of 1840 (1838-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The "Conditions prescribed to submitting highlanders", issued by general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), on 15 June 1840, obliged the Chechen auls to refuse shelter to members of the resistance and to hand over people who had escaped the empire's power. Point 8 prescribed: "Not to give refuge in their auls to abreks, murids and unsubdued highlanders" (abrek - the imperial label for a highlander declared an outlaw; murids - the imam's disciples and warriors); point 11: "To hand over all Russian prisoners and runaways staying in the mountains" - by runaways the empire meant its own soldiers and serfs who had gone over to the highlanders[1]. Handovers went on even before the decree, under the pressure of the winter expeditions: the imperial historian Yurov recorded of the outcome of the December 1839 march of general Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, through Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya): "97 abreks, 7 prisoners and two runaways were handed over", and of the January 1840 march along the Michik river - the auls "handed over 30 abreks"[2]. June 1840 C1165 "Constriction of Chechnya from all sides": blockade, secret war, punitive expeditions and the Sunzha Line (1840-1846) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The empire demanded that Chechen communities hand over soldiers who had fled to them from the imperial army, and set salt as the price of that surrender. Minister of War Chernyshev, in an official service letter (otnoshenie) of 6 September 1842, conveyed to general Golovin, commander of the Separate Caucasus Corps (head of the imperial troops and administration in the Caucasus), the order of emperor Nicholas I: the local command was to ""demand the return of the servicemen who had hidden among the highlanders who had declared their submission to us"", and from the communities that had not submitted to obtain the surrender through need - ""to endeavour to induce the unsubmitted to hand over deserters in exchange for salt""[1]. The emperor expressly forbade ransoming the fugitives with money: the payment for the people handed over was access to the salt the empire kept under embargo. June 1860 C1169 Suppression of the 1860-1861 uprisings, the execution of Baysangur, and the shooting of the zikrists near Shali (1860-1864) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations After the shooting near Shali the empire demanded that the Chechen societies hand over the survivors. On 26 January 1864 Loris-Melikov, head of the Terek oblast, assembled the naibs and "honorable" residents in the Groznaya fortress: the historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova writes - he "announced to the assembled Chechens that they were obliged to hand over all the zikrists [followers of Sheikh Kunta-Haji]. A final deadline was set - 1 February, after which the head of the oblast threatened to commence military operations. He also forbade the performance of zikrist rites"[3]. The historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov quote the demand verbatim: "...to assist in restoring the order disrupted by the zikrists...", and record the ban on the "loud" zikr, compliance with which was to be watched over by the clergy and the village elders[4]. February 1919 C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army In February 1919 the Volunteer Army demanded, through the Mountain government, the handing over of all Red Army men sheltering in Chechnya: "About 700 people were indeed prepared for handover, but this action met the resolute resistance of the Goity Soviet and the open discontent of the people," write historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov (the Goity Soviet - the soviet of the village of Goity); General Shatilov reported: "...unrest is taking place among the Chechens, as part of them do not want the Bolsheviks handed over"[4]. The demand to hand over "all Red Army men, Bolsheviks and abreks" entered the April ultimatum as well[4]. July 1925 C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army On 8 September 1925 Soviet aviation dropped eight one-pud bombs - 16 kilograms each, like a round of a modern 120 mm mortar - on Nozhay-Yurt, to force the village to hand over Gibertiev, the former head of the district militia[5]. Urus-Martan was coerced in the same way: historian A. Yu. Lashkov writes that after artillery fire and bomb strikes "the leadership of Urus-Martan yielded and handed over the bandits on 9 September"[6]. Of the representatives of the local authorities the instruction on mass searches, issued for the operation by the staff of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB), says: they are brought into the removal as those "obliged to point out the dwellings of persons subject to removal, as well as those persons (relatives and others) with whom the person subject to removal may be hiding"[7] - the community itself was made the executor of the removal. The price of this demand is named by historian E. F. Zhupikova: "By force of the highland custom of hospitality, the population of Chechnya, even if it was hostile to the leaders of the insurgents and the chiefs of the bandits, could not hand them over to the authorities. Breaking the custom would have disgraced the highlander for many generations and would have threatened his clan with blood vengeance from the man he had handed over"[8]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References В. title: Imposition of Alien Governance, technique T0151
content: Imposition of Alien Governance The occupation administration artificially deprives subordinated societies of the right to self-governance, appointing loyal representatives of foreign elites over them. Unlike the creation of puppet governments (T0037), this technique does not aim to simulate a civil conflict or to create the appearance of a legitimate local authority. The use of alien overseers is employed by the metropole for open domination, the destruction of the Indigenous people's traditional social ties, and the uninterrupted mobilization of resources. ID: T0151 ⓘ Tactics: Seizure of Governance, Persistence ⓘ People: Nokhchi (Chechens) Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 15 June 2026 Last Modified: 15 June 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1661 C1122 Establishment of Alien Governance and the Mobilization of the Nokhchi for the Crimean Campaigns (1661–1676) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy maintained the regime depriving the subordinated societies of the Nokhchi (the Okochans) of autonomy, officially formalizing the transfer of power over them to a new feudal lord loyal to the metropole: in 1661 Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich issued a charter of grant to the Kabardian prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky, instructing him «to be prince over the Okochans and over the Cherkas who serve us, the great sovereign, on the Terek, and to administer and judge them in military organization and in all our affairs»[1]. April 1858 C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "in 1867 Major General Prince Tumanov was appointed head of the Middle military otdel, while of the eight heads of the mountain okrugs six were colonels and two were majors"[2]. The head of the Terek oblast united civil, military and Cossack authority in one pair of hands and, in the words of the same historians, could against the highlanders "at his own will use... arms and raise against them the troops and Cossacks subordinate to him, hand highlanders over to a military court and administratively expel 'undesirable elements' from the oblast"[2]. From September 1866 the viceroy received the right to replace highlanders in the posts of pristavs (superintendents appointed by the empire) with incomer officers - historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova records the result: for a long time highlanders could rise no higher in the administrative system of the Terek oblast than the office of village elder[3]. The elders themselves were hand-picked by the authorities and sworn to "unquestioning execution... of all instructions and demands of the administration"; the population was left no choice - "The local authorities did not consider it possible to grant even the right to elect aul elders, since they 'found no sufficient guarantees that this would not entail serious inconveniences in the matter of governing the highlanders'"[3]. The court system was crowned by the same officers: in 1862 an oblast Main People's Court was created, all of whose members were appointed by the head of the oblast, and in 1870 - okrug "Mountain verbal courts" chaired by officers of the administration; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov conclude: "Thus the court system created for the highlanders of the Terek oblast was not merely not removed from the control of the military authorities but, on the contrary, directly subordinated to them"[2]. The 1895 regulation on village communities handed the right of assembly to a limited number of "elected representatives", and the okrug head could strip an "elected representative" of his office and dissolve the entire village assembly[2]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Кушева.
