title: Territorial Marking with Imperial Symbols, technique T0158
content: Territorial Marking with Imperial Symbols Aggressors may consolidate the seizure of land with material signs of their own power: crosses and foundation stones at the moment of occupation, monuments to conquerors, memorial plaques and stelae, coats of arms, places of worship raised on the sites of other peoples' sanctuaries. Unlike the renaming of place names, which operates in speech and on the map, a sign occupies physical space and can be removed only by hand. It declares the seizure irreversible and dates the history of the place from the arrival of the metropole: the pedestal of the monument to Bohdan Khmelnytsky in Kyiv (1888) bore the inscription "To Bohdan Khmelnytsky, one and indivisible Russia", while the plaques on the monument to Muravyov-Amursky in Khabarovsk (1891) listed those "who took an active part in the annexation of the Amur region to Russia". ID: T0158 ⓘ Tactics: Persistence, Legitimization of Domination ⓘ Peoples: Nokhchi (Chechens), Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 1 August 2026 Last Modified: 1 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1801 C0038 Creation of the Little Russian Governorate-General (1801–1811) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government In 1804-1811 the Russian Empire erected a cast-iron Monument of Glory in the center of Poltava in memory of its victory over the army of Charles XII on 27 June 1709 - with the city's own money and to a design sent from St. Petersburg. By the imperial decree to the Senate of 11 September 1804, "On leaving the villages formerly owned by the city of Poltava under state administration and on releasing the income collected from them to the local Governor-General for the erection in Poltava of a monument in memory of 27 June 1709," the city's revenues were assigned to the monument: "the community of Poltava citizens, through a petition submitted to Governor-General Prince Kurakin, has designated all these revenues for the construction in Poltava of a monument in memory of the day unforgettable for Russia, 27 June 1709, and so we command: the revenues now due for payment, as well as those henceforth collected in favor of this city, shall be released to the local Governor-General until the monument that has been begun is completely finished"[1]. By a second act, the imperial rescript of 9 May 1805 to the Governor-General of Little Russia, "On the erection of a monument in commemoration of the victory won at Poltava by Emperor Peter the Great," the emperor sent a ready-made design and ordered construction to begin: "I forward to you herewith the plans for this monument, drawn up here, charging you... to proceed with its erection on site, except for the bronze ornaments belonging to it, which will be made separately here and delivered to their destination"[1]. That is, Poltava pays, while Petersburg decides what the sign on its land will look like - down to the bronze, which is cast there and shipped ready-made. The monument was founded on 27 June 1804, the cast-iron column was raised in May 1809 under the direction of Moskvin, an engineer of the Luhansk works, and the whole ensemble was opened on 27 June 1811, for the next anniversary of the battle[2][3]. On the medallion of the upper square of the pedestal, inside a serpent ring between two quivers, stood "June the 27th, 1709," and on the opposite side - "Finished in 1809"[2]: the date of someone else's victory was made into the date of the place itself. Both inscriptions, together with the bronze bas-reliefs, disappeared in 1901 - the pre-revolutionary survey records it tersely: "This inscription and the preceding one were destroyed in 1901, and at the same time the bronze bas-reliefs that surrounded them were taken by persons unknown"[2]; they were restored only during the capital repairs of 1953[3]. The monument still stands in Poltava: as of August 2026 it is listed as a monument of national significance under heritage protection number 160010-Н[4], the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance recommended dismantling it in a letter of 29 July 2024[5], but decisions on monuments of national significance are made by the government, and the list of such decisions as of 20 May 2026 does not include the monument[6]. April 1858 C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations On 15 March 1873 the coat of arms of the Terek oblast was approved: "In a black shield, a silver wavy bend to the right. An Imperial standard on a golden staff. The shield is crowned with the ancient Tsar's Crown and surrounded by golden oak leaves joined by the Alexander ribbon"[7]. Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova reads the meaning of the sign thus: the silver bend is the Terek, which had long been a border, and now "both its banks were united by the Imperial standard, and the Terek became fully Russian - such is the basic meaning of this coat of arms"[7]. The draft coat of arms of the city of Grozny was made by B. V. Köhne, an official of the Heraldry Office: on an azure shield a silver mountain between two golden sea lilies, and in the dexter canton - the arms of the Terek oblast[7], so that the city's emblem carried the imperial symbol of the oblast. The land was marked with the figure of the conqueror as well. The first monument to Yermolov in Grozny was "the carefully preserved dugout in which he lived during the founding of the Groznaya fortress"[7], and later a bronze bust of the general was set up by the dugout. What this sign meant, Ibragimova puts thus: the bust recalled the most tragic years of the conquest of the Caucasus and was a symbol of the dramatic fate of the mountain peoples, and the monument to the general who "with barbaric cruelty exterminated whole peoples in the name of the conquest of the Caucasus" became for Chechens "a kind of 'eyesore'"[7]. The sign outlived the empire: under Soviet rule the monument "was blown up by night with enviable regularity and just as regularly restored by night"[7]. January 1888 C0065 The Bohdan Khmelnytsky Monument (1888) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government On 11 July 1888 the Russian Empire unveiled the Bohdan Khmelnytsky monument on Sophia Square in Kyiv - a sign of "unity" with Moscow: on the left side of the pedestal stood the dates "1654-1888," counting the city's history from the Pereiaslav Rada[8]. The committee for its construction was headed by Mikhail Yuzefovich[8] - an official of the Kyiv educational district and author of the memorandum that formed the basis of the Ems ukase of 1876[9]. The conference convened over that memorandum, sitting with Yuzefovich's participation, resolved "not to permit the import into the empire, without special authorization of the Main Administration for Press Affairs, of any books or brochures whatsoever published abroad in the Little Russian dialect," and "to forbid the printing and publishing in the empire of original works and translations in that dialect, with the sole exceptions of: a) historical documents and monuments and b) works of belles-lettres" - the latter permitted only in Russian orthography and from a manuscript reviewed by the censorship[10]. Under the decree of the Council of People's Commissars of the Ukrainian SSR of 7 May 1919 on removing from squares and streets the monuments erected to tsars and tsarist minions, two of the three inscriptions were knocked off the pedestal; the remaining one was ordered removed by Hrynko, chairman of the Kyiv gubernia executive committee - academician Yefremov recorded this in his diary on 6 February 1925 - and in the end the side plaques were replaced with blank ones, while "Bohdan Khmelnytskyi 1888" was carved on the front stone[8]. May 1909 C0109 The "Historical Path" (1909–1911) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government In 1911 the Russian Empire erected a monument to princess Olha in Kyiv - on a site the city had allotted two years earlier for a monument to Shevchenko. In May 1909, the Kyiv city duma allotted the square on Mykhailivska Square for a monument to Taras Shevchenko[11]. Zilov, the trustee of the Kyiv educational district, wrote confidentially to governor-general Trepov that Shevchenko should not be placed opposite a "Russian governmental institution" and that "it would be necessary to erect a monument to one of the figures of Russian history"[11]. Out of this letter grew the program of the "historical path": on 7 April 1910, colonel Steletsky, secretary of the Kyiv section of the Imperial Russian Military-Historical Society, submitted a memorandum with a queue of eight monuments - princess Olha, Oleh, Yaroslav, Volodymyr, Volodymyr Monomakh, Sviatoslav, "prehistoric Kyiv" and Nestor the chronicler[11]. On 15 March 1911, the duma, with 68 of 72 councilors present, gave the society the site between St. Sophia Cathedral and St. Michael's Monastery - 46 votes against 22 - and at the same session overturned its own decision of 1909, moving the site of the future Shevchenko monument to the Karavaivska intersection: 41 against 24[11]. At first the duma rejected the concrete design as insufficiently "artistically monumental," and a month later permitted only a temporary model to be put up[11] - that is, they agreed to place a makeshift on the seized site, so long as it was occupied. The monument was unveiled on 4 September 1911: princess Olha in the center, to the left the apostle Andrew pointing at the Kyiv hills, to the right the seated Cyril and Methodius[12][13]. The model was sculpted by Ivan Kavaleridze and Petro Snitkin, the architect was Valerian Rykov, and the project was led by the sculptor Fedir Balavensky[14]; the historian Ihor Hyrych notes the paradox - the author of the imperial monument turned out to be "one of the 'Ukrainomaniacs' - a future outstanding sculptor and film director, and then a beginning artist, Ivan Kavaleridze"[15]. Cast on the pedestal was: "A Gift of the Sovereign Emperor to the City of Kyiv. In the Year of Our Lord 1911" - the tsar's cabinet did indeed give ten thousand rubles for the monument, and the Kyiv merchant Mohylevsky contributed another thousand[12][11]. Below, on the pedestal of the princess herself, stood: "She was the first from Rus to enter the Kingdom of Heaven; her the sons of Rus praise as their initiator"[12] - the baptism of Rus was being written into the imperial genealogy right on the stone. In 1919 the statue was thrown off its pedestal and buried, split in two, beneath the monument itself; in March 1923 the remaining figures were removed, and in March 1926 the communal department of Kyiv ordered the concrete cleared away for good[12][11]. In 1996 the statue was dug out from under the flowerbed and the monument was recreated from the old sketches, this time in marble[14]. January 1911 C0110 The Alexander II Monument in Kyiv (1911) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government The Russian Empire erected in Kyiv the largest monument to Alexander II in the entire empire. The gratitude on the pedestal was voiced not by Ukraine and not by Kyiv but by the "Southwestern Krai" - the empire's official name for the Ukrainian lands west of the Dnipro[16]. The monument, by the Italian sculptor Ximenes, was unveiled on 30 August 1911 on Tsarskaya Square, between the entrance to the Merchants' Garden and the building of the Merchants' Assembly; the unveiling was timed to the fiftieth anniversary of the abolition of serfdom and held in the presence of emperor Nicholas II, the Bulgarian tsar Ferdinand and prime minister Stolypin, who two days later, on the evening of 1 September, was mortally wounded in the Kyiv theater[17]. The money for the monument was raised by an all-Russian subscription, 200 thousand rubles[18]. The central pedestal bore the coat of arms of the empire, the double-headed eagle, and the inscription "To the Tsar-Liberator, the grateful Southwestern Krai. The year 1911"; on the lower pedestal was a bas-relief of peasants giving thanks for the abolition of serfdom[18]. The krai comprised the Kyiv, Volyn and Podillia governorates[16], which after the suppression of the Polish uprising of 1830-1831 were merged into the Kyiv governorate-general (1832-1914), whose task, according to the Encyclopedia of the History of Ukraine, "consisted in the liquidation of the political, socio-ethnic and cultural distinctions of the krai and the intensification of the russification of its elite - the szlachta"[19]. The monument joined a row: the Kyiv Nicholas I (1896), Alexander III (1909), Alexander II (1911), Stolypin (1912) - the historian Ihor Hyrych calls this the pre-revolutionary monument boom and adds that the erection of the monument to princess Olha and the planned subsequent monuments were handled by the Kyiv section of the Imperial Russian Military-Historical Society, nine-tenths of which consisted of officers of the Kyiv military district, and its secretary, colonel Steletsky, in a memorandum to the governor-general of 7 April 1910, laid out the queue of future sculptures - from Olha and Oleh to Nestor the chronicler[15]. Hyrych sums up the outcome of those same years thus: in that time the Ukrainians put forward one monument, to Shevchenko, and were not allowed to erect it, while their opponents managed to put up "at least half a dozen monuments asserting Russianness and negating the Ukrainian national idea"[15]. September 1939 C0081 Annexation and Sovietization of Western Ukraine (1939–1941) G0010 USSR S0008 Government The sign of the new order goes up within the very first weeks: Soviet troops took Lviv on 22 September 1939[20], and already in October, in the city center, on the islet in the middle of today's Svobody Avenue, rose the monument to the Stalin Constitution - a huge vertical composition of columns entwined with red banners, on a wooden frame, with five sculptural groups (a Red Army soldier, a worker, a mother with a child, a female student, and an old Hutsul with a boy) and inscriptions in Ukrainian, Polish and Yiddish symbolizing the "friendship of peoples" according to the articles of the Stalin constitution[21][22]. The sign has named authors: the sculptor Serhii Lytvynenko and the Kyiv artist Mykhailo Dmytrenko, who arrived in Lviv in 1939 in the "landing party" of Soviet artists whose task was the implantation of socialist realism; possibly the authors merely adapted to the site a design produced in Moscow, and it was executed by the sculptors Yevhen Dzyndra and Andrii Koverko[21]. The monument stood until 30 June 1941 and vanished with the arrival of the Germans[21]. January 1954 C0087 The Ideological Campaign of the "300th Anniversary of Reunification" and the Transfer of Crimea (1954) G0010 USSR S0008 Government The jubilee was fixed with a material sign in Pereiaslav in the Kyiv region, on the very square where the rada had taken place in 1654. The sign went up in the course of the jubilee reconstruction of the town ordered by the republic's authorities: "in connection with the preparation for the celebration of the 300th anniversary of the reunification of Ukraine with Russia," the Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR allocated 20 million rubles for the reconstruction of Pereiaslav-Khmelnytskyi, the reconstruction plan was developed under the direction of the architect Volodymyr Zabolotnyi, and in May 1954, "on the square where the historic Pereiaslav Rada took place (now Reunification Square), an obelisk with a memorial plaque was erected"[23]. On the plaque, beneath a relief of Bohdan Khmelnytsky, a text is cast: "On this square, on 8 (18) January 1654, the Pereiaslav Rada took place, which, expressing the will of the Ukrainian people, unanimously adopted the historic decision on the reunification of Ukraine with Russia"[24]. The sign did not merely mark the spot: it declared the decision unanimous and expressive of the people's will, fixing this version in bronze on the very square where it all happened. January 1958 C0053 Creation of a Single "Soviet People" (1958–1970) G0010 USSR S0008 Government The material sign of the "merging of nations" was erected in Pereiaslav in the Kyiv region, the city of the Pereiaslav Rada: "on 8 October 1961, a majestic monument in honor of the 300th anniversary of the reunification of Ukraine with Russia was unveiled on B. Khmelnytsky Square"[23]. The authorities unveiled the sign themselves: according to the newsreel Radianska Ukraina No. 49, the opening rally was addressed by Petro Shelest, first secretary of the Kyiv obkom of the CPU, and Pankratov, a secretary of the Moscow obkom of the party - the metropole spoke at the unveiling in its own voice[25]. The composition consisted of two female figures representing Ukraine and Russia and three bas-reliefs with medallions: "a torch, 1654; a hammer and sickle in the rays of the sun, 1917; the Order of Victory, 1945"[26]. The sign's purpose is recorded in its own protection passport: "The monument is a symbol of the eternal, unbreakable friendship and the indestructible monolithic unity of the fraternal peoples - Ukrainian and Russian…"[27]. Four years after the unveiling, the sign was taken under state protection by the resolution of the Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR of 21 July 1965 No. 711 "On the approval of the list of monuments of art, history and archaeology of the Ukrainian SSR"[28][29]. The pedestal bore the inscription "Forever together - forever with the Russian people"; in early December 2021 it was removed by unknown persons[30], and the monument itself was dismantled on 7 July 2022 - by an order of the Ministry of Culture that struck the monument, protection No. 5894-Ko, off the register "due to the loss of the subject of protection"[31]. February 2022 C0103 Full-Scale Invasion (from February 24, 2022) G0011 Russian Federation S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations From April 2022 the Russian occupation administrations marked the seized territories with imperial signs - in stone and on paper. In Kherson oblast more than 110 Lenin monuments had been dismantled before the invasion, with practically none left; after the occupation the invaders erected ten new ones: the first in Henichesk in April 2022 - the first Lenin monument on Ukrainian territory since 2014 - and at the end of that same month a monument was returned to its pedestal by the city council in Nova Kakhovka[32]. In Mariupol on 5 May 2022 a monument to a woman with a red flag was unveiled, and the ceremony was published in his Telegram channel by Andrei Turchak, secretary of the general council of "United Russia"; the Square of the Warrior-Liberators, named in honor of those who freed the city from the Nazis, was given back its Soviet name of "Lenin Komsomol Square" by the occupiers[33]. In parallel the occupation administration papered the territory with banners: in Kherson and Nova Kakhovka hung Russian-language billboards reading "Russia is here forever!," "Kherson - forever with Russia," "Kherson is a Russian city," and for them they bought, for twenty cents on a stock-photo site, a picture by the Ukrainian photographer Anna Pasichnyk - her son Yaroslav with a friend in vyshyvankas in a rapeseed field near Kyiv - painting a Russian flag in behind the children's backs[34]. In Balakliia in Kharkiv oblast the occupiers pasted over a city banner: first they hung "Ukraine and Russia are 'one'" on top of it, then a poster with a tricolor reading "We are one people with Russia!". On 10 September 2022 Ukrainian soldiers tore the tricolor down - and beneath it emerged the lines of Shevchenko that had stood there through the entire occupation: "Fight - and you shall prevail! God is helping you! Truth is with you, glory is with you, and holy freedom!"[35]. The signs held only until de-occupation: on 11 November 2022, a "Russia is here forever" poster in liberated Bilozerka in the Kherson region was torn down by local residents - the video was published by the Telegram channel "Nikolaevsky Vanek"[36]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Собственная Е.И.В. канцелярия (изд.). title: Sham Trials, technique T0160
content: Sham Trials Aggressors may give reprisal the form of justice by creating and using sham trials: the outcome is predetermined and the defense is absent or ornamental. The forms vary - extraordinary and field courts-martial with a day allotted to a case, closed quasi-judicial bodies passing sentences in absentia and by lists, and show trials staged for the public. Passing sentences without "a regularly constituted court affording all the judicial guarantees" is a war crime (Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions; Article 8(2)(c)(iv) of the Rome Statute, under which the International Criminal Court delivered its first conviction in 2024). ID: T0160 ⓘ Tactics: Defense Impairment, Legitimization of Domination ⓘ People: Nokhchi (Chechens) Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 6 August 2026 Last Modified: 6 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: October 1905 C1175 Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations From 10 January 1906 the Russian Empire introduced field courts-martial in the Terek oblast - to them were handed over "...persons who have committed murder, brigandage, robbery and attack on a sentry or military guard, as well as armed resistance to the authorities and attack on the ranks of the troops and the police and on all officials in general..."; during the work of these courts, until 19 April 1907, 195 people in the Caucasus were sentenced to death and another 47 condemned to katorga[1]. April 1920 C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services On 9 May 1924 the Soviet Union, by a secret resolution of the Presidium of the Central Executive Committee (TsIK), gave the OGPU "the right of extrajudicial reprisal against bandits and their accomplices, namely: expulsion from the given locality, confinement in a concentration camp for a term of up to 3 years, and the application of the supreme measure of punishment - shooting", and prescribed that the republics declare localities "unfavorable in respect of banditry", where the GPU organs "are entitled to decide at their own discretion any case of banditry"[2]. The Chechen authorities already in that same May telegraphed the center: "Sanction the creation of a tribunal or a political troika"[3]. The troikas that went to work, "composed of an official of the procuracy, the GPU and the first party leader, — as a rule, passed sentences in absentia — on the basis of the submitted documents, often without even questioning the accused. Of any participation of a defense in the proceedings there could be no talk"[1]. July 1925 C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The instruction on mass searches, issued for the operation by the staff of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB), establishes that until the end of the investigation the arrested are concentrated at the staffs of the OGPU district groups, and of what follows point 19 says: "The procedure for conducting the investigation and the further routing of the arrested is provided for in the regulations on the troikas for the extrajudicial examination of cases"[4]. The "Main Tasks of the Special Operational Groups of the OGPU", approved by Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU for the krai, Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, and Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, include the same procedure directly in the list of tasks: "The removal of the counter-revolutionary, bandit and other criminal anti-Soviet element... the registration of the same, the conduct of the investigation and the extrajudicial examination of their cases and their transportation to the place of destination"[4]. Through this procedure passed 183 of the more than three hundred arrested in the course of the operation - the investigation of their cases ended in extrajudicial shooting[1]. The OGPU had received the right of extrajudicial reprisal a year earlier - by a secret resolution of the Presidium of the TsIK of 9 May 1924 (campaign C1176); the operation's instruction applied it to the arrested. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Я. title: Use as Cannon Fodder, technique T0134
content: Use as Cannon Fodder Aggressors may use unarmed, untrained, or deliberately poorly equipped members of the colonized people (civilians or forcibly mobilized persons) for frontal assaults. This technique is used to directly and physically deplete the enemy's ammunition, reveal its concealed firing positions, and clear minefields with human bodies. Unlike the use of a "human shield" (T0111), where people serve as passive cover to protect the aggressor's troops, here the colonized population is actively used as free, single-use expendable material ("cannon fodder") to preserve the personnel reserve of the metropole's troops. ID: T0134 ⓘ Tactics: Extraction of Benefits, Defense Impairment ⓘ People: Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 27 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: June 1941 C0082 Scorched Earth Tactics and Criminal Mobilization (1941–1945) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army The use of untrained conscripts as expendable material: they were "thrown into combat often at once, without undergoing military training in reserve units, sometimes unarmed, not even changed into military uniform (hence the name)"[1]. The scale is visible from a single episode: "after the Red Army first took Kharkiv in the spring of 1943, about 15 thousand people aged 15 to 45 were mobilized into it and sent to the front without training," with "1 rifle per 5-10 men"[1]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Р. title: Seizure of Power Through Election Manipulation, technique T0133
content: Seizure of Power Through Election Manipulation The aggressor uses the legitimate democratic mechanisms (elections, congresses, parliamentary procedures) of the victim state to seize power from within. Unlike the holding of fake referendums in already occupied territories, this technique is applied to still sovereign, independent institutions. Through the infiltration of agents, falsification of representation quotas, forgery of mandates, and bribery of delegates, the aggressor artificially forms a majority. The goal is to compel a legitimate body of power to vote, in a formally lawful manner, to renounce sovereignty or transfer powers to forces controlled by the metropole. ID: T0133 ⓘ Tactic: Seizure of Governance ⓘ People: Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 26 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: November 1917 C0071 Failure of the Political Seizure of the UNR in Kyiv (November – December 1917) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0020 Controlled Opposition An attempt to convert an electoral minority into a procedural majority at the congress. Actual support was negligible: in the Constituent Assembly elections "across the country as a whole the Bolsheviks gathered less than 24% of the votes, and in the Ukrainian gubernias only 10%"[1]. Hence the wager on capturing representative bodies: the Central Committee of the RSDLP(b) declared outright that "the transfer of government from the hands of one soviet party into the hands of another party is secured without any revolution, by a simple decision of the Soviets, by a simple re-election of deputies to the Soviets," while the All-Russian Central Executive Committee's decree of 4 December 1917 "On the right of recall of delegates" provided the mechanism for such a replacement[1][2]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Лариса Якубова. title: Total Destruction of Infrastructure, technique T0105
content: Total Destruction of Infrastructure Aggressors may deliberately and massively destroy the settlements of an indigenous people - homes, hospitals, schools, houses of worship, life-support systems - up to complete destruction. The people are deprived of housing, livelihood, and the physical environment of life on their own land. ID: T0105 ⓘ Tactics: Seizure of Governance, Defense Impairment ⓘ Peoples: Nokhchi (Chechens), Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1617 C1120 Punitive campaign and the devastation of the Nokhchi mountain communities (1617–1618) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations During the punitive campaign, the military detachments burned entire auls to the ground: in a petition to Tsar Mikhail Fyodorovich, the Kabardian prince Sunchaley Yanglychevich Cherkassky reported that they «burned down and utterly ruined many Shibut and Kalkan and Erokhan and Michkiz kabaks»[1]. January 1709 C0014 Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1709) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army Complete destruction of the Sich's buildings and neighboring fortifications: "the neighboring kurins were also burned and slaughtered"; "All the buildings were destroyed, as Menshikov wrote: 'To lay waste all their places, so that this treasonous nest be utterly uprooted'"[2]. January 1722 C1129 Suppression of the Uprising, Military Intervention, and Forced Formalization of Subjecthood (1722) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Regular Army of the Russian Empire destroyed the settlements and the food supply base of the highlanders: historian Sh. B. Akhmadov states that a tsarist detachment "came to Enderi and completely devastated and burned it, leaving nothing but ashes behind"[3], while during the August 1722 raid "3 thousand houses were destroyed and the grain in the fields was burned"[3]. January 1732 C1132 Armed Uprising on the Plain, General Douglas's Expedition, and the Rout of Colonel Koch's Punitive Detachment (1732) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Regular Army of the Russian Empire physically eliminated a highlander settlement: historian Sh. B. Akhmadov states that the detachment under the command of Colonel Koch «entered the village of Chechen on July 7, burned it down completely, and began hastily withdrawing»[3]. January 1807 C1140 Bulgakov's Punitive Expedition: Devastation of Chechen Villages and Coercion into Allegiance (1807) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire burned the villages of the Nokhchi, depriving the inhabitants of shelter and means of subsistence. General Ivelich reported that the village of Bolshaya Chechenskaya Ataga was "consigned to fire" by the detachment of the commander of the Caucasus Line, General Bulgakov, while the remaining inhabitants, "whose villages were destroyed by fire," agreed to subjecthood[4]. January 1813 C1142 Punitive devastation of the Nokhchi villages along the Sunzha and pitting neighboring peoples against them under Rtishchev (1813-1816) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire razed and burned Nokhchi villages. The imperial historian Potto writes that Colonel Eristov, having crossed the Terek, after a stubborn battle burned and razed «several villages along the Sunzha»[5]. January 1817 C1021 Destruction of the Nokhchi Villages along the Sunzha and Erection of the Groznaya Fortress in Their Place (1817–1818) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Regular Army of the Russian Empire demolished Chechen villages to clear ground for a fortress. Historian D. A. Khozhayev records the destruction of eight villages: to make way for Groznaya, "eight flourishing Chechen villages (Bugun-Yurt, Amirkhan-Kichu, Kuli-Yurt, Sorochan-Yurt, Sunzha, N. Chechen, Topli, Alkhanchu) were destroyed"[6]. September 1819 C1144 Devastation of the Kachkalyk villages of the Nokhchi and displacement of their inhabitants beyond the mountains after the Dadi-Yurt terror (1819) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire wiped Nokhchi villages off the face of the earth. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that following Dadi-Yurt, the Kachkalyk villages of Isti-Su, Noiberdy, Alleroy, and others were "taken by storm and destroyed"[6]. General Yermolov writes in his "Notes" that Noyen-Berdy and Allayar-Aul were "utterly devastated"[7]. The imperial historian Potto confirms that "both villages were completely devastated"[8]. March 1820 C1145 Night Attack on the Aul of Topli, Burning of Germenchuk, and Coercion of the Nokhchi to Fell Their Own Forests (1820) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The imperial historian Potto writes that after the night attack the aul of Topli was left as "smoldering ruins," and at the close of the campaign the troops "advanced forward, burned Germenchug, and drew back to Groznaya," even though the aul stood empty[8]. March 1821 C1146 Suppression of the Nokhchi Uprising: Devastation of Villages and Forced Forest Felling by Grekov (1821-1822) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that the expedition of Grekov, commander of the left flank of the Caucasian Line, "destroyed… two auls — Shali and Malaya Ataga"[6]. The imperial historian Potto confirms: on March 1, 1821, the troops "destroyed completely" the village of Oisungur, and in February 1822 Grekov "burned the villages of Shali and Malye Atagi"[8]. January 1826 C1149 Destruction of the Refugee Aul of Uzeni-Yurt, Extortion of Hostages from Geldigen, and Capture of Samashki Residents at Harvest (1826-1827) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army On January 10, 1827, the troops of General Laptev, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, razed the village of Uzeni-Yurt on the bank of the Argun, whose inhabitants had fled across the river. The imperial historian Potto acknowledges: «the village of Uzeni-Yurt, with all its property... was destroyed to its foundations»[9]. The village had served as home to people whose former auls had been exterminated by troops in Yermolov's punitive campaign of 1826 and who had refused to resettle under the conqueror's control. January 1826 C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that after February 17, 1826, Yermolov's troops «ravaged and destroyed the auls of Lesser Chechnya - Urus-Martan, Roshni, Gekhi, Belakai, Daut-Martan, and Shelchikhi», and by the end of the campaign «flourishing villages had been destroyed»[6]. General Yermolov himself, in a report to Emperor Nicholas I dated May 28, 1826, confirmed: during the storming of Urus-Martan «the village was burned», Bolshaya Roshni was «put to the torch», and the village of Shali, whose inhabitants «give an amanat, asked for time, and deceived», he «ordered to be destroyed»[10]. The imperial historian Volkonsky specifies that Shali stood empty by the time the troops arrived: Yermolov «did not find a single inhabitant there: all had scattered through the forests», after which he «burned their dwellings»[11]. September 1830 C1152 Burning of Lowland Chechnya by Velyaminov's Expedition: Demolition of Villages from the Sunzha to Mairtup, Seizure of Astemir's Family, Collective Penalties Imposed on Chechen Villages, the Cutting Down of Fleeing Inhabitants of Dzulgai-Yurt, and Destruction of Winter Stores (1830-1831) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In December 1830 – January 1831, General Velyaminov's troops razed and burned the villages of lowland Chechnya: Kiter-Yurt, Pkhan-Kichu, Edin-Yurt, Daut-Yurt, Engeli, Uzeken-Yurt, Besenber with its hamlets, Avtury, Geldigen, and Mairtup with the surrounding auls. The imperial historian Potto wrote: Kiter-Yurt "was immediately given over to the flames," "over the following two days the Butyrsky and Tarutinsky regiments burned the village of Pkhan-Kichu," "along the way they burned two more unsubmissive villages: Edin-Yurt and Daut-Yurt," the troops "managed to exterminate one more aul, Engeli," the regiments "burned the unsubmissive village of Uzeken-Yurt," "exterminated in the vicinity the aul of Besenber, with all the hamlets adjoining it," and on January 21, 1831, "the same fate befell Maiortup itself"[9]. The submission offered by the villages of Avtury, Geldigen, and Mairtup, together with the handing over of hostages, Velyaminov rejected, demanding the impossible — the surrender of all Russian captives and fugitives — in order to preserve a pretext for exterminating the villages: submission, as Potto admits, "was not at all part of Velyaminov's designs, as he understood the necessity of punishing these auls cruelly"[9]. August 1832 C1155 Extermination of 61 settlements of lowland Chechnya and mountainous Ichkeria by Rosen's troops, burning alive of the defenders of Germenchuk, and extortion of hostages from 80 villages (1832) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army From August 22 to September 23, 1832, the troops of corps commander Rosen razed dozens of villages of Chechnya and Ichkeria: Belgatoy and Dzhan-yurt, the houses of the six-hundred-household Germenchuk, Shali (except for 11 households), Alkhan-yurt, Sala-yurt, Katar-yurt, Lyalsin-yurt, Nazari-yurt, Uzden-yurt, Uruzbey-yurt, Khyzin-Erzo-yurt, Anzeli-yurt, Chingaroy-yurt, Said-yurt, Anto-yurt, Askhor-yurt, Taba-yurt, Kudish-yurt, Mairtup, Shoni, Tsentoroy, the hamlet of Khamer, Ali-yurt, Bey-Bulat-yurt, Bachin-yurt, Khelboyn-yurt, Benoy, and others. Rosen reported to Minister of War Chernyshev on the dispatch of Colonel Shumsky, by whom "Alkhan-yurt, Sala-yurt, Katar-yurt, Lyalsin-yurt, Nazari-yurt, Uzden-yurt, Uruzbey-yurt and Khyzin-Erzo-yurt have been exterminated"[12], and summed up the result himself: "Of unsubmitted villages, 61 have been exterminated"[12]. Historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "The general’s troops burned Benoy and other Chechen villages"[6]. January 1835 C1156 Covert reconnaissance of Chechnya by Rosen's topographers and the devastation of Zandak by Pullo's detachment: capture of 31 inhabitants and seizure of livestock (1835-1836) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army On August 23, 1836, the detachment of Colonel Pullo, chief of the Sunzha fortified line, ravaged the aul of Zandak on the Yaman-su River. Corps commander Rosen reported to the Minister of War on the destruction in the aul of the houses of murids and of "other principal adherents of Tashev-Hajji"[12]. The Chechen writer Abuzar Aydamirov, in his "Chronology of the History of Checheno-Ingushetia," recorded: "Punitive expedition of Colonel Pullo to the auls on the Yaman-Su River. Destruction of the aul of Zandak"[13]. December 1836 C1158 Extermination of the Inhabitants of Kishkeroy-Yurt by Pullo's Detachment: 76 Killed, 40 Captured, Village Burned with Its Stores (December 1836) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army On 29-31 December 1836, Pullo's detachment completely destroyed Kishkeroy-Yurt: "the village of Kishkeroy, consisting of 63 households, with a considerable stock of grain and hay, was put to the torch", and on withdrawing on 31 December Pullo "marched out of Kishkeroy-Yurt, having set fire to the houses that remained undestroyed"[14]. January 1837 C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Feze's expedition through Lesser Chechnya on 23-29 January 1837 destroyed housing and livelihood outright. The expedition journal, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, records: "Having burned Shalazh-yurt", the troops "destroyed the winter quarters... and the dwellings of the Chechens on both banks of the Shalazha", and "on the way back more than a thousand saklias were burned along the Martan and Tengin gorges" (saklia - a highlander's house)[12]. February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Feze's spring tour (February-April 1837) destroyed the housing and winter livelihood of the Chechen communities. Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 23 February 1837: on 5 February "our troops annihilated the auls of Akhoy-yurt and Lyumik-yurt lying on the way and the khutors of the hostile Chechens"; on 9 February Seid-yurt and Avtur were annihilated[12]. In the March march up the Dzhalka, according to the report of 12 April, "the four auls they had abandoned were occupied and annihilated without resistance. Then the troops penetrated into the thick of the forest and destroyed the kutans (winter shelters for livestock)"; on 26 March the troops were destroying kutans near Shali, and Birzul's column did the same along its own route[12]. November 1838 C1164 Forcing Chechnya into submission after the fall of Akhulgo and suppression of the general uprising of 1840 (1838-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In 1839-1840 the imperial troops burned dozens of Chechen settlements. In the May 1839 invasion of Ichkeria (mountainous south-eastern Chechnya) the imperial officer Milyutin, a participant of the march, recorded day by day: "The nearby aul of Balansu was found abandoned by its inhabitants and given to the flames", "All the auls lying on either side of the road (Nake-Yurt, Tsezyn-Irzau, Doba-Yurt) were found abandoned by their inhabitants and given to the flames", and of the rout on 12 May of Sayasan, the residence of sheikh Tashu-Hadji (in 1834-1836 the imam of Chechnya, leader of the Chechen resistance): "The fortification was devastated, and the village given to the flames"[15]. In the January 1840 march the troops of general Pullo, who commanded the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), wiped out two auls: the imperial historian Yurov - "the auls of Kazbek-Yurt and Batash-Yurt, populated mostly by relatives and namesakes of Shuaib-Mulla, which met the detachment with weapons in hand. After a minor skirmish both villages were levelled to the ground"[16]; historian D. A. Khozhayev adds: "The Russians burned the Benoy hamlet of Gurzhiyn-mokhk and the neighbouring auls of Zandak-Ara and Genderghen, and retreated"[6]. In summer 1840 the detachment of general Galafeyev, who had taken over the troops of the left flank, burned the auls of Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya): historian D. A. Khozhayev lists the destroyed Bolshoy Chechen, Dudu-yurt, Akhshpatoy-Goyta, Chunguroy-yurt, Urus-Martan, Gurak-Roshni, Khazhi-Roshni, Taib and Achkhoy - the troops marched on, "leaving behind them destroyed and burned villages"[6]; the detachment's journal of military operations confirms the route and adds Peshkhoy-Roshni[17]. In autumn the same detachment burned Greater Chechnya (the lowland eastern part of Chechnya): the imperial survey of 27 October 1840 records - "on 3 and 4 October the troops... burned both villages" (Shali and Germenchuk), "on 7 October the detachment burned 5 hamlets attached to the aul of Shali", and of Said-Yurt, the hamlet of Ersenei and the village of Avtury on 10 October: "gave them to the flames and annihilated the houses and all the property of the inhabitants"[14]. Muhammad Tahir al-Qarakhi, Shamil's chronicler (Shamil - the imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest), recorded that the inhabitants of Shali and Germenchuk abandoned and burned their own villages on Shamil's order long before the troops came: "Shamil ordered them to burn those ancient, well-settled and beautiful villages. It was hard for the lower Chechens, but they did it nonetheless" - part of the imperial burnings went through villages already empty; of Said-Yurt he gives the mirror version of the fight: the murids (the imam's disciples and warriors) "fought them and slew a great number of them. The murids put the Russians to flight"[18]. In the November marches of general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line, Gekhi and the auls along the Sunzha were devastated - historian N. I. Pokrovsky: "On 27 October Grabbe marched into Lesser Chechnya, devastated Gekhi, on 4 November laid waste the auls situated along the Sunzha"[19]; the imperial historian Yurov recorded: "During the rearguard action general Galafeyev managed to take by fighting and annihilate to its foundations the village of Mirti-Irzau", then on 13 November Germenchuk with its hamlets was destroyed, on 15 November - Lachi-Yurt and Indi-Yurt, on 17 November the troops seized and burned Batash-Yurt, the home of Shuaib-Mulla (naib - the deputy of imam Shamil in Greater Chechnya)[16]. June 1840 C1165 "Constriction of Chechnya from all sides": blockade, secret war, punitive expeditions and the Sunzha Line (1840-1846) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In 1841-1846 expeditions wiped out Chechen settlements by the dozen. The Aukh village of Kishen the troops of general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), destroyed over three days: the imperial historian Yurov recorded - "by evening the village and its orchards existed no more; out of the heap of charred ruins rose only two mosques and two saklias... spared at the request of Dukai-qadi" (saklia - a highlander's house; qadi - a Muslim judge)[16]. In the march to the Assa river at the end of September 1841 the detachment, according to Yurov, "took by fighting and destroyed 8 auls" - among them Gapurgoy-Yurt, Adilgeri-Yurt, Sha-Yurt - and "the stores of maize and hay were burned"[16]. In the October expedition of 15-30 October 1841 Phan-Kichu, Shalazhi, Magoma-Irzau, Magoma-Yurt, Terga-Yurt, Shuaib-khutor and the auls near Goyta were burned; on 16 October Nurikoy-Yurt was destroyed - Yurov calls it "the most populous and richest Chechen aul"[16]. In December 1846 the troops burned out the Aldy hamlets and the auls of Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya). The imperial officer Poltoratsky, a participant of the expedition, recorded on 15 December 1846: "at the order of the column's commander all the saklias around us burst into flame" (saklia - a highlander's house)[20]. The result of the sweep he summed up thus: "The goal of the expedition in Lesser Chechnya was achieved in full... the plain of Lesser Chechnya in the triangle between the fortresses of Groznaya, Vozdvizhenskaya and Zakan-Yurt has been cleared completely of dwellings and forests"[20]. January 1847 C1166 "Death sentence" for Lesser Chechnya: the massacre of Duba's hamlet, forest clearings, fortresses, annihilation of the population and stanitsas on the sites of burned auls (1847-1851) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The empire destroyed the auls and hamlets of Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya) blow after blow. In November-December 1847 Golen-Goyta and the aul of naib Saib-dula (a deputy of Imam Shamil, leader of the highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest) were destroyed: imperial officer Poltoratsky, a participant in the winter expedition of 1847-1848, wrote of the burned highlander houses (saklias) - "the charred skeletons of saklias and, on the ground, blackened thick pools of blood and human corpses scattered everywhere recalled the rich aul of Golen-Goyta that had existed so recently," and of the aul of Saib-dula: the column "took the aul by storm, annihilated everything in it and burned it to the ground"[20]. On the night of 17 February 1850, under an order of the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus conveyed by the journal of military events of General Ilyinsky - "to annihilate there the dwellings of the harmful population stubborn in its insubmission" - the detachment of Colonel Sleptsov burned the hamlets of Muzuroyev and Nekhloyev and the aul Yasan-yurt: "Few of the inhabitants managed to save themselves... Having finished the annihilation of the hamlets and the aul in two hours' time, Colonel Sleptsov began his withdrawal"[21]. On 15 June 1851 "a series of hamlets and auls" of the Gekhi gorge was annihilated[19], and on 16 November 1851 - the aul Dakhin-Irzau: General Kozlovsky's report notes "the turning to ashes of the aul Dakhin-Irzau with enormous stores of grain and hay"[21]. January 1852 C1167 "Neither plow nor sow": the pogrom of Chechnya, organized famine, the buying-up of elites and the institutions of subjugation (1852-1857) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The auls of Greater Chechnya (the lowland eastern part of Chechnya) were burned out throughout the period. On 6 January 1852 Avtury was burned - imperial historian Volkonsky, a participant in the pogrom, wrote: "The aul Avtury had at that time up to nine hundred households and belonged to the number of the richest auls," and of the detachment's withdrawal: "all the auls and hamlets that lay on the path of our retreat blazed up like their metropole"[22]. On 27 March 1852, at the storming of the aul of naib Talgik (a naib is a deputy of Imam Shamil), "the aul itself was turned into a heap of ashes and ruins"[22]. In December 1852 the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus ordered Baryatinsky, who commanded the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), to destroy Khan-Kala - Volkonsky conveys the order: "the commander-in-chief insistently ordered Prince Baryatinsky to take this aul and raze it from the face of the earth," and the execution: "The aul, numbering ninety-five houses, was given to the flames, and by the evening of that same day not one sound stone remained of it"[22]. The result of 1853 was summed up by Vorontsov, viceroy and commander-in-chief in the Caucasus: in a letter to the Emperor of 1-20 March 1854 he reported that Baryatinsky "took possession of the Michik, cut a clearing of enormous width through the Qachqalyq ridge down to the plains of Greater Chechnya and annihilated the greater part of the villages that still remained unsubdued along the Michik and other streams in the direction of Umakhan-yurt"[21]. In January 1854 the auls along the rivers Dzhalka and Khabi-Shovdan were devastated - the imperial chronicle of "outstanding events" counts the resettlement of "418 families of Chechens"[23]. January 1857 C1168 Forest clearings and famine: Yevdokimov's conquest of Chechnya (1857-1859) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army General Yevdokimov, who commanded the troops of the left wing of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on Nokhchi land), recorded in the journal of military operations of the winter of 1857 that he sent General Mishchenko down the Khizy-Shavdon, "instructing him... to annihilate auls, so as to take away from the Chechens the very thought of the possibility of remaining at the site of their former dwelling"[24]. The execution is recorded there as well: "Major-general Mishchenko burned all the auls and hamlets in the area assigned to him; a multitude of those who had submitted came out to him... up to 400 households, under the cover of part of the troops... sent to Umakhan-yurt"[24]. To the report on this campaign Emperor Alexander II replied with approval "for the completely successful conclusion of the 1st period of the winter campaign"[24]. In November 1857 the same journal summed up the expedition against Salatavia, bordering on Chechnya: "Salatavia has been devastated and burned, so that its inhabitants will now have to settle at the sites of the former Salatavian auls along the Sulak"[24]. Having taken Vedeno, the capital of the Imamate - Shamil's state - the empire destroyed the fortress: "Occupied on 1 April 1859 by the tsarist troops, the Vedeno fortress was completely destroyed within five days"[6]. June 1860 C1169 Suppression of the 1860-1861 uprisings, the execution of Baysangur, and the shooting of the zikrists near Shali (1860-1864) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In June 1860 the troops devastated the aul of Dzhumsoy, abandoned by its inhabitants: according to a July 1860 report from the commander of the troops of the Terek oblast to the Viceroy, it was "devastated to the ground, and part of the crops annihilated"[24]. The outcome of Kundukhov's operation in the winter of 1860-1861 is summed up in his own report, quoted by the historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova: "All the buildings, in the auls as well as in the khutors, have been burned to the ground... the hay not only in the auls but even on the very summits of the mountains has been annihilated by fire, at which the inhabitants themselves marveled, seeing that in inaccessible thickets and on the heights the hay was burning"; General Bazhenov reported on 29 November 1860: "Today I have finished with the Termoy people. All the auls are destroyed. In Ezi you cannot even recognize the place, so thoroughly has it been taken apart"[25]. In all, according to the historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov, "15 villages and a multitude of mountain khutors were left destroyed"[26]; the historian D. A. Khozhayev writes: "about 15 auls implicated in it [the uprising] were destroyed... Benoy was burned once again"[6]. April 1877 C1172 "Mow Down Everything, Beat and Hang Without Mercy": Suppression of the 1877 Uprising and the Executions in Grozny (1877-1878) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The order of Colonel Lokhvitsky of 17 July 1877 for the Cheberloy uchastok (administrative section) prescribed: "to raze to the ground the villages of Nizheloy, Rigakhoy and Nuy-Khoy"[27]; historian A. I. Ismailova sums up: "The auls and crops of the Cheberloy uchastok were destroyed wholesale; the same fate befell many auls of the Shatoy and Evdokimovsky uchastoks. The inhabitants hid in the forests"[27]. In October 1877, on the way back from the Simsir hamlets, historian D. A. Khozhaev records: "the Russians burned and destroyed Zandak and, for the second time, the village of Benoy - everything, down to the last house, including the mosques, they leveled to the ground"[6]. October 1905 C1175 Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations In 1911 the Russian Empire demolished the Chechen hamlets of two okrugs: "A forcible demolition was begun of all the hamlets built 'without permission' (and there were no others here) in the Vedeno and Grozny okrugs"[26]; Chechen hamlets "were repeatedly demolished, including under the pretext of 'punishment' for sheltering abreks"[26]. February 1919 C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army In its March offensive along the railway the Volunteer Army destroyed villages to the ground: "for several days stubborn battles went on, in the course of which the villages of Berdykel and Ustar-Gordoy ended up completely destroyed, and a number of other villages were captured"[26]. The year's count is kept by the Soviet survey cited by historian E. F. Zhupikova: 21 destroyed auls (27 in another publication of the same source) with 15 thousand dead[28]. The Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov, who wrote of these events in emigration, gives both the motive and a list by name: the highlanders' desire "to arrange their state life at their own discretion" Denikin construed as "national Bolshevism", "hence the policy of burning auls and the extermination of the unsubmissive highlanders", and "to break the resistance of the Chechens and the Ingush, Denikin burned to the ground dozens of the largest centers of Chechnya-Ingushetia - Ekazhevo, Dolakovo, Alkhan-Yurt, Chechen-Aul, Ustar-Gardoy, Gudermes, Gerzel-Aul, Stary-Yurt and others" (Ekazhevo and Dolakovo are Ingush villages)[29]. July 1925 C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Disarming Chechnya, the troops of the USSR destroyed the villages that had not met the ultimatum, up to complete demolition: the aul of Khakmedy - more than 300 households - was destroyed entirely, in the aul of Dai 20 houses were destroyed, Urus-Martan stood for three days under artillery fire and air strikes. A surviving companion of imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky - the spiritual head of the resistance in Dagestan and Chechnya, whom the troops pursued into the mountains - related in 1936 in the Warsaw journal Severny Kavkaz: "Then the fire was transferred to the nearest auls, of which the aul of Khakmedy (more than 300 households) was completely destroyed"[30]. The aul of Dai, the center of resistance of the fifth combat sector, historian A. Yu. Lashkov describes from the documents of the military archive: "From the shelling and bombings the aul of Dai suffered substantially: 20 houses turned out destroyed, there were a small number of human casualties"[31]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "...the aul of Urus-Martan was subjected to artillery shelling and air strikes for three days, the aul of Dai was bombed three times, for two days artillery shelled the auls of the Zumsoy society"[26]. June 1941 C0082 Scorched Earth Tactics and Criminal Mobilization (1941–1945) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army The 1941 scorched-earth tactic under the directive of the USSR Sovnarkom and the Central Committee of 29 June 1941: "In the forced withdrawal of Red Army units, drive off the rolling railway stock, leave the enemy not a single locomotive, not a single railcar"[32]; the Dnipro hydroelectric station was "destroyed at the beginning of the Great Patriotic War… (see the Directive of the USSR Council of People's Commissars and the Central Committee of the VKP(b) of June 29, 1941)"[33]. February 2022 C0103 Full-Scale Invasion (from February 24, 2022) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army The practice of "urbicide" - the deliberate erasure of entire Ukrainian cities (for example, Mariupol), the destruction of infrastructure, and the entombment of the dead in the foundations of ruins[34]. The blowing up of the Kakhovka dam on 6 June 2023: "the breach of the dam at the Kakhovska Hydroelectric Power Plant in June 2023 resulted in massive flooding downstream, triggering an environmental disaster that has already had catastrophic effects on communities across the region," while "the flooding killed 34 civilians (32 in Kherson region and 2 in Mykolaiv region)" on Ukrainian-controlled territory alone[35]. The scale of the disaster on the very first day: "about 16 thousand people on the right bank of Kherson region are in the critical zone," with 80 settlements under threat of flooding[36]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Кушева. title: Resource Exploitation, technique T0102
content: Resource Exploitation Aggressors may establish an uncontrolled and exhausting regime of exploitation of the natural riches, infrastructure facilities, and productive potential of the seized region. Pumping out mineral resources, illegal resource extraction, and using food reserves in the interests of the metropole deprives the Indigenous people of the economic base for independent existence and redirects all the region's wealth toward the enrichment of the colonizer. ID: T0102 ⓘ Tactic: Extraction of Benefits ⓘ Peoples: Nokhchi (Chechens), Ukrainians Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 21 April 2026 Last Modified: 9 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: January 1704 C0017 Forced Labor on Imperial Construction: The Ladoga Canal (1704–1725) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0008 Government Shifting the upkeep of the mobilized onto the subjects themselves: Cossacks dispatched to the imperial construction sites were left without supply and "suffer great want from hunger, having neither food for themselves, nor winter quarters, nor fodder for the horses"[1]. Workers for state construction the tsar simply ordered to be "taken from Ukraine, from those towns that are under your authority"[1], while at the works themselves people perished "from back-breaking labor, hunger and the harsh climate"[2]. January 1817 C1021 Destruction of the Nokhchi Villages along the Sunzha and Erection of the Groznaya Fortress in Their Place (1817–1818) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Regular Army of the Russian Empire shifted the cost of the imposed military service onto the Indigenous population itself. Imperial general Yermolov testifies in his "Notes" that the men levied by requisition were sent out "with their own arms and at their own expense"[3]. November 1838 C1164 Forcing Chechnya into submission after the fall of Akhulgo and suppression of the general uprising of 1840 (1838-1840) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The "Conditions prescribed to submitting highlanders", issued by general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), on 15 June 1840, obliged the Chechen auls to hand over the working cattle and transport of their households for the empire's use: at the first demand of the pristav (a superintendent appointed by the empire) to provide arbas (two-wheeled carts) and donkeys. Point 4 prescribed: "At the pristav's demand to provide arbas or donkeys for hauling loads"[4]. February 1845 C1173 Colonial oil: the seizure of the Grozny subsoil and the rent of the Cossack host (1845-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The Terek Cossack Host of the Russian Empire leased out the seized Chechen lands to oil companies and lived on rent from another people's subsoil: in 1899 about 21.9 million of the 26.22 million puds of total output were extracted on the host's lands, and in that year alone the companies paid the host 631.8 thousand rubles[5]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: the largest owner of the oil-bearing plots turned out to be the host itself; it did no extraction of its own, and the usual terms of a lease were 150 rubles a year per desiatina (a desiatina is a little over a hectare) plus "from 2 to 6 kopecks for every pud of oil extracted"[5]. Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova records the dynamic: the host's capital grew from 400 thousand rubles in 1877 to 3 million in 1900 - "This was the result of receiving income from the oil-bearing lands"[6]. The scale was set by the field itself: on 27 August 1895 well No. 7 of Akhverdov's company gave "a gusher of incredible force, yielding up to 1 million puds a day... The roar and the smell of oil could be sensed 15 versts from the field"[7]. January 1890 C0066 Industrial Colonization and Resource Exploitation of the South (1890) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government The Ukrainian regions became the empire's main raw-materials donor: "In 1910 coal extraction amounted to 1 billion poods, and in 1913 – 1.5 billion poods. Over this time the Donbas's share in the empire's coal industry grew from 67% to 74%… Before World War I, Ukrainian metallurgy produced 2/3 of the pig iron smelted in the empire"[8]. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Татьяна Таирова-Яковлева. title: Sexualized Violence, technique T0161
content: Sexualized Violence Aggressors may use sexualized violence as a weapon: rape during punitive operations and sweep operations, sexual torture of detainees, the treatment of captive women as spoils. Such violence targets more than the victim - it terrorizes and humiliates the entire community. Rape, sexual slavery and any other form of sexual violence is a war crime and a crime against humanity (Articles 7(1)(g) and 8(2)(b)(xxii) of the Rome Statute; Article 27 of the Fourth Geneva Convention). ID: T0161 ⓘ Tactics: Defense Impairment, Persistence Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 6 August 2026 Last Modified: 6 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram

title: Collective Punishment, technique T0159
content: Collective Punishment Aggressors may apply collective punishment: for the actions of individuals, reprisals fall on the entire community - villages and districts are subjected to monetary levies, troops are quartered at the residents' expense, families and relatives are exiled, dwellings are demolished, hostages are taken. The prohibition is entrenched in every key codification of the law of war: Article 50 of the Hague Regulations on the Laws and Customs of War on Land (1899, 1907) forbids general penalties imposed on the population for the acts of individuals; Article 33 of the Fourth Geneva Convention (1949) expressly prohibits "collective penalties and likewise all measures of intimidation or of terrorism"; Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions (1977) extends the prohibition to non-international armed conflicts, and the ICRC study of customary international humanitarian law (2005, Rule 103) records it for conflicts of any kind. ID: T0159 ⓘ Tactics: Defense Impairment, Persistence ⓘ People: Nokhchi (Chechens) Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 6 August 2026 Last Modified: 6 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: September 1830 C1152 Burning of Lowland Chechnya by Velyaminov's Expedition: Demolition of Villages from the Sunzha to Mairtup, Seizure of Astemir's Family, Collective Penalties Imposed on Chechen Villages, the Cutting Down of Fleeing Inhabitants of Dzulgai-Yurt, and Destruction of Winter Stores (1830-1831) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1830, General Velyaminov introduced collective property levies on Chechen villages that bore no responsibility for the actions of others: for the driving off by Chechens of ten head of cattle from the stanitsa of Chervlennaya, he "immediately ordered that ten head of cattle likewise be taken from the inhabitants of the two villages of Braguny and Novy-Yurt, past which the party had traveled, and returned to the Cossacks"; for the driving off of a herd of horses in the Nogai steppe, "Braguny once again paid with exactly the same number of head"; and Shakh-Girei, the owner of Novy-Yurt, was confined to a casemate — a prison cell of the Groznaya fortress — for the inaction of the village watch. This was recorded by the imperial historian Potto[1]. February 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army By the April 1837 raid on the Gertli settlement the troops of General Feze imposed a collective property levy on the whole village: according to Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 30 May, on top of the livestock taken during the raid "a fine of 132 head of livestock was imposed on the settlement"[2] - the settlement paid as a whole, with no regard to the personal involvement of its residents. October 1905 C1175 Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Following the Chervlyonnaya conferences of 1905-1906 the Russian Empire established a mechanism of circular monetary responsibility: fines on the guilty, "and in the event of their financial insolvency - the penal sanctions passed to the village community to which the guilty party belonged"[3]. Starye Atagi was fined twice for sheltering its fellow villager, an abrek - 3, then 6 thousand rubles; the same village was ordered, within three days, to hand over "100 rifles, two thousand cartridges and 500 daggers", to give up the abreks Tomayev and Khorsiev who were sheltering in the village, and "to collect funds for equipping the village police station with telephone communication"[3]. Tsatsan-Yurt in 1908 paid a "contribution" for undelivered weapons - 7 thousand rubles[3]. In 1911, by order of the Viceroy, "100 thousand rubles were exacted" from the entire Chechen population of the Grozny and Vedeno okrugs in compensation to those who had suffered "...during the attack of Zelimkhan's band"[3]. July 1925 C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Even before the operation the village assemblies together with the revkoms (unelected committees installed in place of elected Soviets - campaign C1176) drew up lists of the "vicious element" - inhabitants noted in robberies; historian E. F. Zhupikova writes: "They and their relatives bore material responsibility for all cases of theft on the territory of Chechnya"[4] - the relatives paid for others' thefts by the fact of kinship and an entry in the list. One could leave the list only by an oath with an obligation to inform: "If the 'vicious element' took an oath that for a year he would not rob and would inform on thieves, he was struck from the list"[4]. When the troops reached the mountains, the destroyed was counted by the same category: as the result of the bombing of 16 auls "119 houses of the 'vicious element' were blown up"[4]; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov confirm the number - "119 houses were blown up"[3]: a house was blown up because its owner was entered in the list. document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { initProcedureList(document.getElementById("techProcs")); }); document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => { // пришли с матрицы конкретного народа — оставляем в фильтре только его // (чекбоксы уже построены initProcedureList: его DOMContentLoaded // зарегистрирован раньше и выполняется первым) const PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH = { "russia/ukrainians": "Ukrainians", "russia/nokhchi": "Nokhchi (Chechens)", }; const container = document.querySelector('#techProcs .people-filter-box'); if (!container) return; const ref = document.referrer || ""; for (const [path, people] of Object.entries(PEOPLE_BY_MATRIX_PATH)) { if (ref.includes('/matrices/' + path)) { const boxes = Array.from(container.querySelectorAll('input[type=checkbox]')); const target = boxes.find(cb => cb.value === people.toLowerCase()); if (target) { boxes.forEach(cb => { cb.checked = (cb === target); }); container.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); } break; } } }); References Потто В..
